presentingComplaint: High-grade fever with yellowish discoloration of eyes and reduced urine output for 3 days
history: 34-year-old sanitation worker presents with abrupt-onset high-grade fever, severe myalgia (predominantly calf muscles), frontal headache, and chills for 6 days. Over the last 3 days he has developed yellowish discoloration of the sclera and skin, dark-colored urine, and progressively decreasing urine output. He reports wading through flood-contaminated water while clearing a blocked drain 10 days ago. No prior liver disease. No alcohol excess. No history of jaundice previously. No rash, no joint symptoms, no recent travel outside the flood-affected city area. No known TB contact. Not on any nephrotoxic medications.
examination: Toxic-looking, icteric, mildly dehydrated. Conjunctival suffusion present bilaterally (without discharge). Marked tenderness over calf muscles on palpation. Mild hepatomegaly (liver span 14 cm, non-tender). No splenomegaly. No rash or petechiae. No lymphadenopathy. Chest clear. No neck stiffness. Alert and oriented, no asterixis.

labs.ast_alt: mildly elevated (2-3x ULN, disproportionately lower than bilirubin)
labs.urinalysis: proteinuria, granular casts, few RBCs, no significant pyuria

imaging: Ultrasound abdomen: mild hepatomegaly, normal biliary tree, no ascites, kidneys normal size with preserved corticomedullary differentiation
differentialDiagnoses: Viral hepatitis with acute kidney injury
Sepsis with acute liver and kidney dysfunction
finalDiagnosis: Leptospirosis (Weil's disease) with jaundice and acute kidney injury
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Leptospirosis
WHO Human Leptospirosis: Guidance for Diagnosis, Surveillance and Control 2003
KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury 2012
stewardship: Empirical therapy for severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease): intravenous penicillin G or ceftriaxone; doxycycline is an alternative for milder disease not requiring hospitalization. Supportive care with fluid/electrolyte management and renal replacement therapy if indicated for AKI. Watch for Jarisch-Herxheimer-like reaction after first antibiotic dose.
contraindications: Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., NSAIDs, aminoglycosides) given AKI
Adjust renally-cleared drug doses to current creatinine clearance
Doxycycline relatively avoided if significant hepatic dysfunction/pregnancy consideration
edgeCases: Anicteric leptospirosis (mild, self-limited) is far more common than the icteric Weil's disease variant presented here
Severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome (SPHS) is a distinct life-threatening leptospirosis presentation not covered in this case
MAT (microscopic agglutination test) remains the reference/confirmatory serologic test; IgM ELISA is a sensitive screening test but confirmatory testing is recommended
LEPTOSPIROSIS is present in the engine disease list as its own id, so acceptableIds correctly maps to it rather than falling back to []
expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag the combination of water/flood exposure, conjunctival suffusion, disproportionate jaundice with only mild transaminase elevation, myalgia with elevated CPK, and AKI as classic for icteric leptospirosis (Weil's disease), recommending empirical penicillin/ceftriaxone and MAT confirmation while excluding malaria, dengue, and enteric fever.
